article.title: How Long Does Champagne Last Unopened?
article.body:
How Long Does Champagne Last Unopened?

Unopened non-vintage champagne is at its best within about three to four years of purchase, and vintage champagne keeps for five to ten years or longer. Drinks House 247 advises storing bottles somewhere dark, cool and steady, ideally 10 to 13°C. Champagne does not expire like food; it slowly loses freshness and fizz.

Most champagne is bought for a moment, then forgotten at the back of a cupboard when the moment moves. Whether that bottle is still worth opening depends on two things: what kind of champagne it is, and where it has been sitting.

Does champagne expire?

Not in the way milk does. There is no date after which an unopened bottle becomes something other than wine. What changes is quality. Over time the fresh fruit fades, the bubbles become softer, and the wine develops nutty, toasty and eventually sherry-like flavours. Some drinkers enjoy that evolution in a good vintage. In a basic non-vintage bottle kept in a warm kitchen, it simply tastes tired.

Most champagne bottles carry no "best before" date. Some houses print a disgorgement date on the back label, which is the most useful clue you have: it tells you when the wine was finished and corked, and so how long it has been ageing since.

How long each style keeps

Style Keeps well unopened What happens with age
Non-vintage brut 3–4 years from purchase Loses freshness and citrus; bubbles soften
Non-vintage rosé 2–3 years from purchase Red-fruit character fades first; colour turns towards onion-skin
Vintage champagne 5–10 years or more Gains brioche, honey and nutty depth if stored well
Prestige cuvées 10–20 years or more Built for long ageing; many are released only when already mature
Demi-sec and sweeter styles 3–5 years Sweetness becomes more caramel-like

These are windows for enjoyment, not cliffs. A well-stored non-vintage bottle at five years is often perfectly pleasant, just different. A badly stored one at two years can already be past its best.

Why storage matters more than age

Three things damage champagne in a bottle: heat, light and movement.

  • Heat speeds up every chemical reaction in the wine. A bottle kept at 22°C next to an oven ages noticeably faster than one at 12°C in a cellar. Repeated warming and cooling is worse still, because it makes the cork expand and contract.
  • Light, particularly sunlight and fluorescent light, causes a fault known as light strike, which gives a cabbage-like, sulphurous smell. Clear bottles are most at risk, which is why some houses wrap theirs in cellophane or gift boxes.
  • Vibration is a smaller factor for a few months, but constant movement, such as on top of a fridge or washing machine, is best avoided for anything you plan to keep.

The ideal is a steady 10 to 13°C in the dark: a cellar, a wine fridge, or the coolest cupboard in the house away from appliances and radiators.

Should you keep champagne in the fridge?

For days or a couple of weeks, yes. For months, no. A domestic fridge is dry, cold and vibrates, and over a long period the cork can dry out and let the wine oxidise. Chill champagne for the occasion, not for storage. A bottle needs around three hours in the fridge to reach serving temperature of 8 to 10°C.

Upright or on its side?

For short-term storage, upright is fine: the carbon dioxide in the neck keeps the cork humid. For keeping a bottle over several years, lying it on its side is the conventional advice, and it is what most cellars do. Either way, the conditions around the bottle matter far more than its angle.

How to tell if a bottle is past its best

You cannot judge from the outside with much confidence, but a few signs are worth checking before a special occasion:

  • A cork that has shrunk or pushed out, or any sign of leaking around the foil, suggests air has got in.
  • A deep gold or brownish colour in a non-vintage champagne that should be pale straw.
  • A flat, soft pour with few bubbles when you open it.
  • Aromas of sherry, stewed apple or old walnuts dominating everything else. This is known as maderisation, and in a vintage champagne a hint of it can be pleasant; in a young non-vintage it means the wine has gone too far.

A tired bottle is not dangerous. It is simply disappointing, and it can still be used for cooking, a sparkling cocktail or a risotto.

Is it worth ageing champagne on purpose?

For vintage and prestige bottles bought from a reliable source, yes, if you have proper storage. For non-vintage brut, the honest answer is usually no. Houses release non-vintage champagne to be drunk on release, blended for a consistent, fresh style. A few extra months will not hurt it, but you are unlikely to improve it at home, and you take on the risk of poor storage. Buy non-vintage for the occasion; save the cellaring for vintage.

Frequently asked questions

How long does unopened champagne last?

Non-vintage champagne is best within about three to four years of purchase. Vintage champagne keeps for five to ten years or more, and prestige cuvées often longer, provided they are stored cool and dark.

Does champagne go off if it is not opened?

It does not expire like food, but it slowly loses freshness and fizz and develops nutty, sherry-like flavours. A badly stored bottle can taste tired within two years.

Can you store champagne in the fridge?

For a few days or weeks, yes. For months, no, because a domestic fridge is dry and can dry out the cork. Store it at 10 to 13°C in the dark and chill it for about three hours before serving.

How can you tell if champagne has gone bad?

Look for a shrunken or leaking cork, a deep gold or brown colour in a wine that should be pale, very few bubbles, and a strong sherry or stewed-apple smell.
